title: California Law Students Explain Confusing Ballot Measures to Voters
summaryZh: 加州麥喬治法學院學生撰寫268頁報告，向選民解說14項州公投提案。
summaryHi: कैलिफ़ोर्निया के कानून छात्रों ने 14 मतपत्र प्रस्तावों पर 268 पेज की रिपोर्ट बनाई।
summaryEs: Estudiantes de Derecho en California explican 14 propuestas electorales en un informe.
summaryJa: カリフォルニアの法科学生、14の住民投票案を268ページの報告書で解説。
summaryEn: California law students wrote a 268-page guide to help voters understand 14 ballot measures.
paragraphs: With a crowded ballot and campaigns making competing claims, law students in Sacramento are trying to help California voters make informed decisions about the 14 statewide propositions on the November ballot.

Students at the University of the Pacific's McGeorge School of Law spent the semester analysing every measure and published their findings in a 268-page report that is freely available online. The school runs a dedicated course on California propositions in every election year, which also teaches students how a statewide initiative is drafted.
On Wednesday evening, the students presented their research at a free public forum, where residents could ask questions. They describe their analysis as detailed and nonpartisan.

Law student Nikki Adkins said the flood of ads, text messages and phone calls can be overwhelming, and admitted that some measures were hard to understand even after two months of study. Voter Art Fong agreed, saying that campaign materials often contradict each other.

Professor Mary-Beth Moylan said Propositions 41 and 42 are attracting particular attention because they are countermeasures to Proposition 40, a so-called 'billionaires tax'. As student Andrew Dale explained, if either countermeasure wins more yes votes than Proposition 40, the tax would be void even if it passes.
In California, people do not only vote for leaders. They also vote yes or no on new laws. These are called propositions. This year, there are 14 of them.
Many voters find them hard to understand. They see a lot of ads and get many messages and phone calls.
Law students at the University of the Pacific in Sacramento want to help. They studied all 14 propositions for a whole term. Then they wrote a long report of 268 pages. It is free on the internet.
On Wednesday night, the students talked to people at a free meeting. People asked them questions.
One student said the laws are hard even for them. Three propositions are about a tax on very rich people.
Law students in Sacramento are helping California voters understand the 14 statewide propositions on the ballot in November.

Students at the University of the Pacific's McGeorge School of Law spent the whole term studying each proposition. They put their findings into a 268-page report, which anyone can read online. The school offers a special class on propositions in every election year.
On Wednesday night, the students presented their work at a free public meeting and answered questions from local people. They say their report does not support any party.

Student Nikki Adkins said voters can feel overwhelmed by ads, texts and phone calls. One voter, Art Fong, said that different leaflets often say opposite things. Adkins added that the measures were difficult even for the students after two months of work.

Three propositions, 40, 41 and 42, are getting a lot of attention because they are about a 'billionaires tax'. Student Andrew Dale explained that if 41 or 42 gets more yes votes than 40, then 40 will not become law, even if it passes.

As Election Day nears and California's ballot fills up with competing claims, a group of law students in Sacramento has taken on the task of untangling the 14 statewide propositions for ordinary voters.

Students at the University of the Pacific's McGeorge School of Law devoted the semester to dissecting each measure, compiling their conclusions into a 268-page report that is freely accessible online. The course, offered every election year, also gives students a close look at how statewide initiatives are drafted.
The students unveiled their findings at a free public forum on Wednesday evening, fielding questions from residents and stressing that their analysis is rigorous and nonpartisan.

Their work appears to fill a real need. Law student Nikki Adkins described the barrage of ads, texts and calls as overwhelming, conceding that even after two months of scrutiny some measures remained hard to grasp. Voter Art Fong complained that rival materials frequently say the exact opposite of each other.

Much of the buzz surrounds Propositions 40, 41 and 42, rival proposals concerning a so-called 'billionaires tax'. As student Andrew Dale explained, should either countermeasure win more yes votes than Proposition 40, the latter would be rendered null and void even if it were approved.

Direct democracy can place considerable demands on voters, and California, with 14 statewide propositions on its November ballot, is a striking example. In response, law students in Sacramento have produced a resource designed to help citizens make informed decisions.

Over the course of a semester, students at the University of the Pacific's McGeorge School of Law examined each measure in depth and published a 268-page nonpartisan report, which is available online free of charge. The course, which runs in every election year, also familiarises students with the process of drafting a statewide initiative.

On Wednesday evening, the students presented their research at a public forum and responded to questions from the community. According to student Nikki Adkins, voters are often overwhelmed by advertisements, text messages and phone calls, and she acknowledged that some measures remained complex even after two months of analysis.

Particular attention has focused on Propositions 40, 41 and 42, which concern a proposed 'billionaires tax'. Propositions 41 and 42 are countermeasures: if either receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, the latter would become void, even if it is approved.
Initiatives such as this suggest that universities can play a valuable role in strengthening public understanding of complex legislation.
